intro: Nine steel spheres, 102 meters tall, arranged as an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times. Built for a world's fair and meant to vanish, the Atomium refused to leave and became the symbol of a city.
page_title: Atomium: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: In January 1955 the engineer Andre Waterkeyn, director of the economic department at Fabrimetal, presented his first project for the centerpiece of the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. His idea was a unit cell of an iron crystal, a body-centered cube of nine atoms, magnified 165 billion times. The architects Andre and Jean Polak transposed the concept into buildable architecture, and the Jambes-Namur Construction Workshops raised it in 18 months on the Heysel Plateau in Laeken. The name Atomium joins the words atom and aluminum, the metal the spheres were first clad in. The brief was a tribute to scientific progress and a demonstration of Belgian engineering skill, and the structure delivered it at 102 meters and 2,400 tonnes of steel, completed less than a month before Expo 58 opened on 17 April 1958.
sections.heading: A crystal magnified 165 billion times

sections.body: The Atomium was designed to last six months, a temporary pavilion for a fair. But its popularity made it a fixture of the Brussels landscape, and its demolition was postponed year after year until the city authorities decided to keep it. The engineering had a close call: the original design had no supports under the three lower outer spheres, but wind-tunnel tests showed the structure would have toppled in an 80 km/h wind, so support columns were added. The three upper outer spheres were never given vertical support and remain closed to the public for safety reasons. Only six of the nine spheres are visitable: the three on the central axis and the three on the lower outer edges.
sections.heading: Built to last six months

sections.body: Each sphere is 18 meters in diameter. Steel tubes 3 meters across join them along the twelve edges of the cube and from all eight vertices to the central sphere, twenty tubes in total, enclosing the stairs, the escalators and the lift. The lift runs in the central vertical tube: it climbs at 5 meters per second, carries 22 people and reaches the top sphere in 23 seconds, which made it the fastest lift in Europe in 1958. The escalators in the oblique tubes include one 35 meter run, among the longest in Europe. The bottom sphere holds the permanent exhibition on the 1950s, Expo 58 and the construction of the building; the top sphere holds the panoramic restaurant, with room for about 140 guests, above the observation deck.
sections.heading: Nine spheres, twenty tubes

sections.body: By the turn of the millennium the Atomium had deteriorated, and a comprehensive renovation was overdue. Jacques Delens and BESIX carried out the work starting in March 2004; the building closed to the public that October and stayed closed until 18 February 2006. The faded aluminum sheets were replaced with stainless steel, which is fitting because stainless steel is primarily iron, the very crystal the building depicts. The meridians of each sphere were fitted with LED lighting that can flash along the meridians, symbolizing the range of an electron around its core, and the German designer Ingo Maurer created lighting installations for the interior. A new reception pavilion with a boomerang-shaped roof went up, and the roundabout at the foot became a concrete esplanade lined with continuous benches. To help finance the 26 million euro renovation, pieces of the old aluminum plates were sold to the public as souvenirs, a triangular piece about 2 meters long fetching 1,000 euros. Then Prince Philippe officially reopened the building on 14 February 2006, and Belgium issued a 2 euro commemorative coin for the renovation, 5 million coins on 10 April 2006.
sections.heading: A stainless steel rebirth

sections.body: The Atomium was built for Expo 58 as a tribute to scientific progress and a symbol of Belgian engineering skill, and it became the defining icon of the atomic age in Europe. It was meant to be temporary; its popularity saved it, and the full renovation of 2004 to 2006 secured its future. Belgium put it on a 2 euro commemorative coin in 2006, 5 million issued, marking the renovation. Today its silhouette is the visual shorthand for Brussels worldwide, the city's emblem on souvenirs, posters and media, and with over 600,000 visitors a year it is the city's most popular tourist attraction: a museum, an art center and a cultural destination.

timeline.text: Engineer Andre Waterkeyn presents his first project for the Expo 58 centerpiece.
Construction of the foundations begins on the Heysel Plateau.
Erection of the steel frame begins.
Completed less than a month before Expo 58 opens: 102 m tall, 2,400 tonnes of steel.
Expo 58; the lift to the top takes 23 seconds, the fastest in Europe.
The 47th Tour de France passes in front of the Atomium in its opening stages.
Full renovation by Jacques Delens and BESIX; aluminum cladding replaced with stainless steel.
Officially reopened by then Prince Philippe.
Opens to the public again after the renovation.
Belgium issues a 2 euro commemorative coin for the renovation, 5 million coins.
